In passive motion scenarios, external forces dictate limb trajectory, rendering muscle-generated innervation irrelevant. This implies that articular cartilage surfaces—subject to deformation during motion—are the primary loci of spatial awareness. The mathematical framework treats this as a constraint satisfaction problem where joint angles θ are inferred from passive displacements P under force F. The sensory system encodes these deformations into a geometric representation, enabling GSE to compute positional states. Meanwhile, GSI employs Bayesian inference to weigh evidence from both cutaneous and articular modalities, with articular signals dominating when cutaneous inputs fail. The failure mode occurs when sensory loss disrupts this dual-channel architecture, forcing exclusive reliance on mechanical cues. Dualities emerge in how mechanical energy translates into perceptual fidelity, with articular surfaces exhibiting higher resolution than cutaneous ones. This supports a layered cognitive architecture where lower-level mechanics inform higher-order spatial reasoning.
